lines.text: Cave painters, Roman cities, Moorish palaces and a world empire, then civil war, dictatorship and a hard-won democracy. This is the story of Spain.
Deep in a cave in Cantabria, Ice Age painters covered a ceiling with bison. Altamira was the first such art the modern world recognised.
Rome made the peninsula its province of Hispania, which gave the empire rulers like Trajan and Hadrian, and gave Spain its Latin tongue.
When Rome fell, the Visigoths took over, ruling Spain from Toledo for more than two centuries.
In 711 Muslim armies crossed from Africa, and al-Andalus was born, a land of Muslims, Christians and Jews, of science, poetry and great buildings.
Soon after, in the mountains of the north, small Christian kingdoms began the long Reconquista, pushing slowly south for nearly eight centuries.
In Cordoba, one of the great cities of the world, the Great Mosque rose with its forest of striped arches. Centuries later a cathedral was set inside it.
In the early twelve hundreds the University of Salamanca was founded, among the oldest in Europe, where scholars would later debate the rights of American peoples.
Above Granada the Nasrid rulers built the Alhambra, a palace of courtyards, fountains and carved plaster, the finest Islamic art in Spain.
Far away in France, the House of Bourbon began as minor lords. One day its branch would wear the crown of Spain, as it still does.
Isabella of Castile married Ferdinand of Aragon, joining the two great Spanish crowns and setting the country on a new course.
In 1478 the Spanish Inquisition was set up to enforce the Catholic faith. It would last until 1834.
With their union, Spain as a single kingdom took shape, the country that would rule an empire and, much later, become a parliamentary monarchy.
Then came 1492, a year that changed everything. First, the Alhambra Decree drove out the Jews of Spain who would not convert.
That same year, sailing for the Spanish crown, Christopher Columbus reached the Caribbean, joining Europe and the Americas for good, and at great cost to their peoples.
And Ferdinand and Isabella took Granada, ending the last Muslim rule in Spain.
The Spanish Empire grew from those voyages, holding much of the Americas and the Philippines. Its silver shaped world trade, and Spanish became a world language.
After the conquest of the Aztecs, New Spain was governed from Mexico City, stretching from Central America to the Philippines.
At home came a golden age. Miguel de Cervantes, soldier and former captive, wrote Don Quixote, often called the first modern novel.
In 1588 Philip the second sent his Armada to invade England. English ships and storms broke it, and many vessels never came home.
At the court of Philip the fourth, Diego Velazquez painted kings, dwarfs and princesses with a truth no one had seen before.
His Las Meninas shows a little princess, her attendants and the painter himself at work, a puzzle of mirrors still argued over today.
A century later Francisco Goya, court painter in Madrid, recorded the horrors of war, and in his deafness painted his darkest works.
In 1805, off the Spanish coast at Trafalgar, Nelson's British fleet destroyed the ships of France and Spain.
Then Napoleon invaded. Spanish soldiers and guerrillas, with British help, fought him for six years and drained his strength.
As the century turned, Antoni Gaudi filled Barcelona with curving buildings and bright tiles, like Casa Batllo and Park Guell.
Pablo Picasso, born in Malaga, would found Cubism with Braque and paint Guernica, the great cry against the Civil War.
In 1882 work began on Gaudi's Sagrada Familia in Barcelona, a church still being built, meant to be the tallest in the world.
Francisco Franco, a general, would lead the Nationalists to victory in civil war and rule Spain as dictator until he died.
In 1899 FC Barcelona was founded, owned by its members and, as its motto says, more than a club.
Three years later its great rival was born. Real Madrid, in white at the Bernabeu, would win more European Cups than anyone.
Salvador Dali, with his famous moustache, painted dreams and melting clocks, and made Surrealism a household word.
In 1936 the country tore itself apart. Germany and Italy backed Franco's Nationalists, the Soviets the Republic, and after three years Franco won.
In 1937 German and Italian planes bombed the Basque town of Guernica, the horror Picasso put on canvas.
Juan Carlos, born in exile, would become king and steer Spain to democracy, facing down a coup attempt in 1981.
A lighter note: in 1945 a scuffle at a parade in Bunol started La Tomatina, where each August thousands pelt each other with tomatoes.
Pedro Sanchez, born in 1972, would lead the Socialists and become prime minister in 2018.
When Franco died in 1975, Spain made its transition, sealed by the constitution of 1978: a democracy under a king.
In 1982 the new Spain hosted the World Cup, and Italy lifted the trophy in Madrid.
Rafael Nadal would go on to win the French Open fourteen times and twenty-two Grand Slams in all, a hero of Spanish sport.
In 1992 Barcelona hosted the Olympics, gathering almost every nation and using the Games to remake its harbour and streets.
In 2004 bombs on commuter trains in Madrid killed a hundred and ninety-three people, the worst terrorist attack in Spain's history.
Six years later came joy: in South Africa, Spain beat the Netherlands in extra time to win its first World Cup.
In 2017 Catalonia held a vote on independence that Spain's courts had banned, and the country faced its deepest crisis in decades.
And in October 2024 torrential rain sent floods through towns around Valencia, killing more than two hundred people.
From painted caves to a modern democracy, Spain's story runs on.
